title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) that measures whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents using gpt-5-mini and a canonical verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed without technical failures (planned episodes 144, completed 144, model calls used 72, artifact count 510). All baseline emulation executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired reduction in undetected-fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; bootstrap seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0). Because the preregistered shared_initial_candidate estimand compares the identical generated candidate with and without verification, a verifier cannot reduce executed faults when the identical candidate already produces no baseline failures; we analyze artifact-grounded causes of this ceiling outcome and give concrete, preregisterable design modifications that would permit measuring verifier utility when baseline error prevalence is non‑negligible.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises to accelerate NetOps workflows but raises safety concerns when generated device-level sequences violate reachability, access‑control, ordering, or workflow invariants. A common mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that pairs stochastic generation with deterministic checking and, where permitted, repair or human review. Prior proposals and prototypes advocate such guarded pipelines, but systematic preregistered paired measurements that compare identical generated candidates executed with and without a canonical verifier are scarce. This paper addresses a narrowly scoped, preregistered research question: does inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM generator and emulator execution materially reduce the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults when the identical generated candidate is evaluated both without and with verification?

Contributions. (1) We preregistered and executed study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 under shared_initial_candidate semantics using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on 72 paired intents (24 per difficulty stratum), producing complete deterministic accounting artifacts. (2) We report the exact confirmatory outcome: no baseline emulator faults and therefore no possible verifier-induced reduction (paired difference = 0.0; CI [0.0,0.0]; p = 1.0), and we explain this ceiling outcome with artifact-grounded diagnostics. (3) We provide concrete, preregisterable alternative designs (independent-generation arms, repair-enabled flows, adversarial seeding, sampling sweeps, multi-model comparisons) that enable non-degenerate inference about verifier utility and demonstrate how the archived execution and analysis artifacts form a reproducible template for those follow-ons.
sections.related_work: LLM-driven intent→configuration translation has been empirically studied in constrained settings where modern LLMs produce plausible device-level configs from operator intent, but these evaluations are often limited to curated task families and vendor-dialect subsets [1]. System and prototype work has proposed multi-agent and tool‑augmented frameworks that embed deterministic checks or domain tools into agentic NetOps workflows [2], illustrating feasible integration points for verifiers in practice. The generate–verify–repair pattern—well studied outside NetOps in code and software repair domains—shows that deterministic validation can enable correctness‑convergent workflows when baseline generator errors are non‑negligible and when repair or resampling is permitted [3]. Canonical formal network-verification approaches (header-space and related reachability/policy analyzers) provide semantics-aware invariants suitable for the verify stage but, in the supplied literature, lack preregistered paired experiments that measure detection performance against executed emulation outcomes [4]. Our study situates itself at the intersection of these strands by providing a preregistered, artifact-grounded paired measurement that isolates verifier detection under shared_initial_candidate semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 and froze the design before executing any runs. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational-fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Confirmatory hypothesis H1 targeted an absolute paired reduction of 0.20; planned sample N = 72 paired intents stratified equally into three difficulty strata (medium/hard/very_hard).

Shared_initial_candidate contract. The execution contract enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent we performed a single initial LLM generation and evaluated that identical candidate in two paired conditions. Baseline: execute the shared candidate in an isolated emulator and record whether an emulator‑observed operational fault occurs. Guarded: run the deterministic verifier on the same candidate; if the verifier flags a violation the guarded outcome is recorded as prevented (no executed fault); otherwise execute the identical candidate and record the result. Under this contract any observed paired difference can only arise from the verifier preventing execution of a candidate that would otherwise fail at emulation.

Model, adapter, and verifier (artifact-grounded). The declared model is gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter and the canonical verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0") configured with the full_intent_constraint_validation rule set. The recorded model parameters include declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini", provider = "openai_responses", max_output_tokens = 2000, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, and temperature = null. The archived temperature = null indicates provider-default runtime sampling semantics were used (it is not evidence of deterministic, temperature=0 sampling). The verifier emits structured validator_traces per episode (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, validation_before/after snapshots, violation_codes, and violation_count); these traces determine guarded decisions.

Task-bank, stratification, and contamination controls. Confirmatory tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each manifest encodes an intent, structured required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty.level. The preregistration specified exact-match contamination checks against public corpora; no confirmatory pair was excluded.

Execution, retries, and analysis. The missingness_plan allowed up to two retries for transient hosted-API errors; all provider events were logged. Execution manifest records: planned_episode_count = 144, completed_episode_count = 144, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 72, artifact_count = 510. The registered analysis pipeline (paired_binary_analysis_v1) computes the 2×2 contingency (guarded × baseline), runs an exact McNemar test when discordants exist, and constructs paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CIs (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Pre-specified subgroup confirmatory comparisons (topology complexity and policy type) use Holm correction when informative.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired estimand isolates verifier detection on identical generated candidates; when those identical candidates produce no baseline emulator faults the algebra of the estimand forces a paired difference of zero. The observed numeric degeneracy (n_11 = 72; paired difference = 0.0; CI [0.0,0.0]; p = 1.0) therefore reflects an internally consistent outcome rather than a procedural error. Artifact-grounded diagnostics attribute this ceiling to three measurable pipeline factors: (1) the deterministic task manifests encoded explicit required_sequence and allowed_touched_fields that constrained acceptable configs; (2) the model (gpt-5-mini) produced candidates that matched those encoded constraints across the synthetic corpus; and (3) the verifier rule set enforced the same manifest constraints. Per-episode validator_traces corroborate this alignment (parsed_command_count = required_command_count and violation_count = 0).

Design and statistical implications. A confirmatory paired test aimed at detecting an absolute reduction (here preregistered 0.20) requires a non-zero baseline prevalence of executed faults to have power. When baseline prevalence is zero, no verifier—even a perfect one—can improve the observed outcome under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For future confirmatory studies that aim to measure verifier detection utility, the task bank should be designed (and preregistered) to yield a measurable baseline error rate, for example by including ambiguous intents, known failure-mode seeds, or adversarial wording.

Preregisterable alternative designs to enable non-degenerate inference. The archived infrastructure supports several preregisterable modifications that change the estimand and permit detecting verifier utility:
- Independent-generation arm: allow separate initial generator calls per condition so the guarded workflow can influence candidate distributions (via resampling or repair) and thereby change execution outcomes.
- Repair-enabled flow: permit verifier-triggered deterministic repair (at most one repair attempt per pair) and execute the repaired candidate to measure end-to-end improvement.
- Adversarial/fault-seeding bank: include intentionally ambiguous or subtle-ordering intents to raise baseline fault prevalence and probe verifier detection under stress.
- Sampling-parameter sweeps and multi-model comparisons: register explicit non-null temperature values and multiple model versions to quantify sampling- and model-sensitivity.
- Blocking-cost arm: measure operational blocking cost when the verifier blocks flagged candidates versus when blocked candidates are repaired and re-executed.
Each of these changes is preregisterable and compatible with the same deterministic accounting and artifact conventions used in this run; adopting them would avoid the algebraic ceiling encountered here.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolates verifier detection but prevents verifier-mediated resampling or repair effects; provider-call audit confirms one shared generation per pair. Construct validity: emulator-observed failures are a conservative surrogate for operational harm and do not capture hardware-specific or traffic-dependent timing effects. External validity: single-model experiments (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a synthetic task bank limit generalization to other models and real-world operational distributions. Sampling-parameter uncertainty: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (provider-default sampling semantics), a residual uncertainty that future preregistrations can remove by specifying numeric sampling parameters.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) under shared_initial_candidate semantics to test whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM-generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and synthetic/emulated task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0; bootstrap 95% CI [0.0,0.0]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate confirmatory outcome is an expected algebraic consequence of the shared_initial_candidate estimand when identical candidates produce no baseline failures. Measuring verifier utility under realistic error regimes requires preregistered designs that intentionally create a non‑negligible baseline error prevalence or that permit verifier-mediated resampling/repair. The archived execution and analysis artifacts provide a reproducible template and concrete starting point for such powered follow-on confirmatory experiments.

Human role: a Research Director selected the NetOps topic family and approved the immutable initial master prompt prior to the lock; no human manually edited technical manuscript content after the lock. Models and orchestration: initial generation used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration) orchestrated via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0") served as the canonical verifier; an isolated emulator executed candidate configurations. Preregistration: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 was preregistered and frozen before observing outcomes. Immutable master-prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Complete execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the manuscript; these artifacts record provider calls, model configuration (temperature = null indicating provider-default sampling semantics), per-episode validator traces, and the deterministic analysis outputs. No human manual manuscript editing occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: the baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit under the shared_initial_candidate estimand.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per-condition generation, multi-sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single-model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.
Sampling-parameter uncertainty: archived execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (provider-default sampling semantics) and thus residual uncertainty about exact sampling behavior.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact-match checks were applied, but private training-data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
